title: How do you design multi-datacenter Kafka replication, and what is the tradeoff between active-active and active-passive?
shortTitle: How do you design multi-datacenter Kafka replication, and what is the tradeoff between active-active and active-passive?

s1_definition.profdef: Multi-datacenter Kafka replication copies data between independent clusters in different regions, usually with MirrorMaker 2 or a managed equivalent, to provide disaster recovery and geo-locality. In active-passive, one region takes all writes and the other is a warm standby you fail over to during a disaster, which is simpler and avoids conflicts but wastes the standby and incurs failover time. In active-active, both regions accept writes and replicate to each other, which gives lower latency to local users and no idle capacity, but you must solve offset translation, loop prevention, and conflicting writes to the same key.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India running two branches in Mumbai and Chennai. Active-passive is like Mumbai doing all the work while Chennai keeps an up-to-date copy of the ledgers in a locked room, ready to take over only if Mumbai floods. Active-active is like both branches serving customers at the same time and constantly couriering copies of their ledgers to each other, which is faster for local customers but risks two branches editing the same account at once and having to reconcile.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use MirrorMaker 2 to replicate between regional clusters, choosing active-passive for simple safe disaster recovery or active-active for low local latency at the cost of conflict handling and offset translation.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Multi-datacenter Kafka replication copies data between independent clusters in different regions, usually with MirrorMaker 2 or a managed equivalent, to provide disaster recovery and geo-locality. In active-passive, one region takes all writes and the other is a warm standby you fail over to during a disaster, which is simpler and avoids conflicts but wastes the standby and incurs failover time. In active-active, both regions accept writes and replicate to each other, which gives lower latency to local users and no idle capacity, but you must solve offset translation, loop prevention, and conflicting writes to the same key.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India running two branches in Mumbai and Chennai. Active-passive is like Mumbai doing all the work while Chennai keeps an up-to-date copy of the ledgers in a locked room, ready to take over only if Mumbai floods. Active-active is like both branches serving customers at the same time and constantly couriering copies of their ledgers to each other, which is faster for local customers but risks two branches editing the same account at once and having to reconcile.

**One line to remember:** Use MirrorMaker 2 to replicate between regional clusters, choosing active-passive for simple safe disaster recovery or active-active for low local latency at the cost of conflict handling and offset translation.

sections.s2_technical:
Kafka's built-in replication keeps copies within one cluster across brokers, but it does not span regions, because stretching the in-sync replica set across high-latency links would cripple write latency. So cross-region copying uses a separate tool. MirrorMaker 2, built on Kafka Connect, is the standard. It runs source and checkpoint connectors that read from the source cluster and produce into the target cluster. It replicates topic data, and crucially it also replicates consumer group offsets and emits checkpoints so a consumer can resume in the other region near where it left off.

A key detail is topic naming and loop prevention. MirrorMaker 2 by default prefixes mirrored topics with the source cluster alias, so a topic `transactions` from the Mumbai cluster appears as `mumbai.transactions` in Chennai. This prevents infinite replication loops in active-active, because each cluster only forwards its own locally-originated topics, not the already-prefixed mirrored ones. You can override this, but then you must configure loop prevention yourself.

Another key detail is offset translation. Offsets are per-cluster, so offset 42 in Mumbai is not offset 42 in Chennai. MirrorMaker 2 writes checkpoint records that map source offsets to target offsets for each consumer group, and the RemoteClusterUtils or the automated offset sync lets a failed-over consumer translate its last committed Mumbai offset into the right Chennai offset, so it resumes without reprocessing everything or skipping data.

Active-passive is the simpler design. All producers and consumers run against the primary region. MirrorMaker 2 continuously copies topics and offsets to the standby. During a disaster you redirect clients to the standby, translate offsets, and resume. The tradeoffs are that the standby capacity sits idle most of the time, failover is a deliberate operation with some data-loss window equal to the replication lag, and you must test failover regularly or it will not work when you need it.

Active-active is the more capable but harder design. Both regions accept writes and mirror to each other. Local users get low latency because they write to their nearest cluster. The hard problems are three. First, loop prevention, solved by the cluster-alias prefix so mirrored topics are not re-mirrored. Second, offset translation, since a consumer reading both local and remote topics must track offsets per source. Third and hardest, conflicting writes: if the same account is updated in both regions at nearly the same time, you can get divergent state, so you either partition ownership so each key is only written in one region, called active-active with data locality, or you use conflict resolution such as last-writer-wins or application-level reconciliation.

A senior nuance is that for money movement, true multi-master writes to the same account are dangerous, so banks usually use active-active for read scaling and locality but pin write ownership of each account to a home region, effectively making it active-passive per key while using both regions fully. Another nuance is that replication lag defines your recovery point objective, so you monitor MirrorMaker 2 lag closely, and you decide the recovery time objective by how fast you can redirect clients and translate offsets.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs Kafka in Mumbai and Chennai. Regulators require that a regional outage must not lose confirmed transactions and the bank must recover quickly. The platform team must design cross-region replication and choose a topology.

Problem 1 — within-cluster replication does not protect against a whole-region outage, and stretching it across regions would make every write slow. This is exactly why cross-region copying with MirrorMaker 2 is needed as a separate layer.

Problem 2 — after a failover, consumers must resume near where they left off, not reprocess days of data or skip transactions. This is exactly what offset translation and checkpoints solve.

Problem 3 — the team debates active-active for low latency versus active-passive for simplicity, and worries about two regions editing the same account. This is exactly the active-active versus active-passive tradeoff, resolved by pinning write ownership of each account to a home region.

The code will model a replication plan that computes the recovery point objective from replication lag, translates a source offset to a target offset using a checkpoint map, and decides whether a given account may be written in a given region under active-active with home-region ownership.

```yaml
#   mumbai->chennai.enabled = true

#   emit.checkpoints.enabled = true
bank:
  topology: active-active
  home-region:
    SAV2001: mumbai      # Rajesh writes in Mumbai
    CUR3001: chennai     # Priya writes in Chennai
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a mirror lag of one thousand five hundred milliseconds, a checkpoint map for a consumer group, and write attempts for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001).

Step 1 — the planner reports the recovery point objective as roughly the replication lag, one thousand five hundred milliseconds. This is the window of transactions that could be lost if Mumbai disappears instantly, because anything newer had not yet been mirrored to Chennai.

Step 2 — on failover, a consumer that had committed Mumbai offset 42 cannot reuse that number in Chennai because offsets differ per cluster. The planner looks up the checkpoint map and translates Mumbai offset 42 to Chennai offset 982, so the consumer resumes exactly there without reprocessing or skipping.

Step 3 — under active-active with home-region ownership, Rajesh's home region is Mumbai. A write for SAV2001 in Mumbai is allowed. A write for SAV2001 in Chennai is rejected and routed to Mumbai, which prevents two regions editing the same account and avoids conflicts.

Step 4 — Priya's home region is Chennai, so her write in Chennai is allowed. Both regions are fully used, but no single account is written in two places at once.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka's own replication keeps copies within one cluster but does not span regions, because stretching the in-sync replica set across a high-latency link would cripple write latency. So for multi-datacenter I use a separate copying layer, typically MirrorMaker 2, which is built on Kafka Connect. It replicates topic data and, importantly, consumer group offsets, and it emits checkpoints so a consumer can resume in the other region near where it left off. It also prefixes mirrored topics with the source cluster alias, which prevents infinite replication loops in a bidirectional setup.

The topology choice is active-passive versus active-active. Active-passive is simpler: one region takes all writes and the other is a warm standby that I fail over to during a disaster. The tradeoffs are that the standby capacity sits idle, failover is a deliberate operation, and the possible data-loss window equals the replication lag, so I monitor that lag and I rehearse failover regularly.

Active-active lets both regions accept writes, which gives local users lower latency and uses all capacity, but it introduces three hard problems: loop prevention, solved by the cluster-alias prefix; offset translation, solved by the checkpoint map since offsets differ per cluster; and conflicting writes to the same key, which is the dangerous one. For money, I never allow true multi-master writes to the same account, so I pin each account's write ownership to a home region. That gives me active-active for locality and read scaling while behaving like active-passive per account to avoid conflicts.

In my National Bank of India project across Mumbai and Chennai, we ran active-active with home-region ownership. Rajesh's account was written only in Mumbai and Priya's only in Chennai, both regions mirrored to each other with MirrorMaker 2, and our recovery point objective was the mirror lag of a second or two. On failover we translated offsets through the checkpoints so consumers resumed cleanly, and we drilled the failover quarterly so it actually worked when regulators asked.
